itinerary.heading: Week by week
itinerary.note: This is a guide to what you can expect to do on program. The order in which activities occur might vary. Itineraries are subject to change.

weeks.title: Tokyo temples, markets & homestay
weeks.body:
Welcome to Japan! You’ll meet your Program Instructors in Tokyo for orientation, then move into a homestay with a Japanese family, gaining firsthand insight into customs, etiquette and daily life.

We visit Senso-ji Temple and Nakamise Street, walk the Imperial Palace gardens, and explore Tsukiji Fish Market and the Ginza and Asakusa neighborhoods. A hands-on workshop and a team-building scavenger hunt with a visit to Odaiba round out the week.
weeks.imageAlt: Busy city street crossing lined with colourful billboards

weeks.title: Kyoto & Nara
weeks.body:
We take the Shinkansen to Kyoto and settle into a traditional ryokan. We visit Kiyomizu-dera Temple and the Higashiyama district, take part in a tea ceremony, and try on kimono for photos.

A day trip to Nara brings us to Todai-ji Temple and its friendly deer. Back in Kyoto we join a cooking workshop, explore Nishiki Market, take a calligraphy or origami workshop and walk through Arashiyama Bamboo Grove.
weeks.imageAlt: Golden pavilion reflected in a pond surrounded by pine trees

weeks.title: Takayama & the Japanese Alps
weeks.body:
We travel to the mountain town of Takayama, known for its samurai heritage and Edo-period streets, and get an introduction to the Japanese Alps. We explore the old town and its morning markets and join a craft workshop.

Then we head into the Alps for a full day of hiking, staying in local lodges or mountain huts and learning about Japan’s relationship with nature and traditional mountain life.
weeks.imageAlt: Quiet street of traditional dark wooden houses

weeks.title: Community engagement & conservation
weeks.body:
We cycle through rural villages and join a local community and conservation project, including forest conservation work.

This part of the program offers a deeper look at Japan’s environmental philosophies, which emphasize harmony between people and nature.
weeks.imageAlt: Clear river winding through forested hills under a blue sky

weeks.title: Hiroshima, Miyajima & farewell
weeks.body:
We travel to Hiroshima to visit the Peace Memorial Park and Museum, a powerful reminder of resilience and hope. A ferry takes us to Miyajima Island to see Itsukushima Shrine and hike Mount Misen.

We wrap up with a group cooking class, learning to make Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, a final reflection circle and presentations, and a farewell dinner to celebrate the friendships and memories made in Japan.

faq.heading: Questions we get about this program

items.q: How fit do I need to be?
items.a: No prior experience is needed, but be ready to give everything a go. Expect plenty of walking, a full day of hiking in the Japanese Alps, cycling through rural villages and a hike up Mount Misen.
A mix of hostels, a traditional ryokan in Kyoto, a homestay with a Japanese family and local lodges or mountain huts in the Japanese Alps.
By private van, trains (including the Shinkansen bullet train) and ferries.

items.q: Will I stay with a host family?
items.a: Yes. Part of the program is a homestay with a Japanese family, giving you firsthand insight into customs, etiquette and daily life.

Tuition covers all in-country transport, accommodation, meals, and the activities and entry fees in the itinerary. It doesn't cover international flights, visas, travel insurance, spending money, optional college credit or optional activities.

items.q: How much spending money should I bring?
items.a: About $100 a week for snacks, laundry, personal shopping and optional activities. It varies from student to student.

items.q: Can I stay in touch with home?
items.a: Yes. We encourage keeping phones on flight mode so you stay present, and wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns. There will also be a photo album that students and instructors can upload photos and video to, so parents and caregivers can stay up to date.

items.q: Do I need a passport or visa?
items.a: Your passport must be valid for more than 6 months after the program ends. All the information you need in regard to visas will be available in your student portal.

safety.heading: For parents: how we keep students safe

items.title: 24/7 Emergency Line
items.body: Parents, students and instructors can reach a real person at any hour. Every call is logged and passed to our on-call staff member by phone.

items.title: Wilderness First Aid & Live Risk Assessment
items.body: All our instructors hold Wilderness First Aid (WFA) certification and have extensive training in group leadership and risk management.

items.title: Accredited Safety Systems
items.body: Our safety systems are assessed and accredited by the Gap Year Association (USA), Year Out Group (UK) and OutdoorsMark (NZ). Students on Go Overseas voted us one of the top gap year providers for safety.

items.title: Insurance & Health
items.body: Comprehensive travel insurance is required, covering medical costs and emergency evacuation. Check vaccinations with your doctor, and pack a first-aid kit and any personal medication. Our instructors can't legally give students any medication.
